title: The Quran's Internal Contradictions
summary: The Quran contains verses that directly contradict one another, requiring Islam to develop the doctrine of naskh (abrogation), which inadvertently destroys the foundational claim that the Quran is the perfect, eternal, uncreated word of God.
challenge: Abrogation (naskh) is taught by the Quran itself (2:106, 16:101), so it is not a hidden embarrassment. It is progressive legislation: God gave rulings suited to the community at each stage, as with the gradual prohibition of wine (2:219, 4:43, 5:90). The Bible does the same when the food laws are set aside (Mark 7:19; Acts 10). Changing a ruling is not contradicting a truth.
response:
The doctrine of naskh is Islam's internal solution to undeniable contradictions within the Quran, but it creates a far more serious problem than the one it solves. Surah 2:106 explicitly acknowledges abrogation: 'We do not abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten except that We bring forth one better than it or similar to it.' This means the Quran contains verses that Allah himself replaced with better versions. But if the Quran is the uncreated, eternal word of God (co-eternal with Allah, as classical Islamic theology (Ash'ari school) insists), then what does it mean for one part of an eternal, uncreated text to be 'better' than another? An eternal, perfect text does not improve. It does not supersede itself. The very existence of naskh proves that the Quran is a historically conditioned document, not a timeless eternal word.

The contradictions requiring abrogation are not peripheral. Surah 2:256 declares 'there is no compulsion in religion', among the most-quoted Islamic tolerance verses. Surah 9:5 commands 'slay the polytheists wherever you find them' and Surah 9:29 commands warfare against People of the Book until they pay jizya 'while they are humbled.' Classical Islamic jurisprudence, across all four major schools, ruled that Surah 9 (revealed last) abrogates Surah 2:256. The 'no compulsion' verse was abrogated by the sword verse. Muslim scholars differ on how many verses are abrogated (estimates range from 5 to 500) but no serious Islamic scholar denies the principle.

The theological damage is fatal: if Allah changes his mind, Allah is not omniscient. If the earlier verses were perfect expressions of divine will, why replace them? If they were imperfect, why were they revealed? If the Quran is eternal and uncreated but contains time-conditioned, superseded commands, the doctrine of the Quran as the uncreated word is internally incoherent. The Christian doctrine of progressive revelation (where the New Covenant fulfills and completes the Old) does not face this problem because Christianity does not claim the Old Testament is co-eternal with God or that it will never be superseded. Islam claims precisely this for the Quran, and naskh demolishes the claim from within.
sources: John Gilchrist, The Textual History of the Quran (1989)
Nabeel Qureshi, No God But One (2016)
rejoinder: Progressive revelation across history is a fair point, and the Bible has it too. But the Bible never claims to be an uncreated text kept eternally on a heavenly tablet. A change of law between covenants fits a God acting in history; a ruling cancelled within one eternal, unchanging book is harder to square with the Quran's claim about itself (85:21-22). Muslim scholars also disagree widely on how many verses are abrogated, which shows the difficulty is real.

title: The Satanic Verses Incident
summary: Early Muslim historians record that Muhammad once recited words honouring three Meccan goddesses and later withdrew them as Satan's insertion. Many classical scholars rejected the story, so it must be handled honestly. But even on the most cautious reading, Surah 22:52 says Satan casts into the recitation of every prophet, which raises the question of how a listener can tell revelation from interference.
challenge: The story fails the standards Muslim scholars apply to every report. Its chains of transmission are broken (mursal) or weak, the disputed words are absent from the canonical hadith collections, and leading authorities such as Ibn Kathir and Qadi Iyad rejected it. Surah 22:52 teaches the opposite of what critics claim: whatever Satan casts, God abolishes, and he makes his verses firm. It is a promise of protection, not an admission of contamination.
response:
The incident is recorded by early Muslim historians, not by enemies of Islam. Ibn Sa'd and al-Tabari (who preserves Ibn Ishaq's account) describe Muhammad reciting, after Surah 53:19-20, words that praised al-Lat, al-Uzza and Manat as 'exalted cranes whose intercession is hoped for.' Sahih al-Bukhari records the closely related scene of Muslims and polytheists prostrating together at the end of Surah 53, though without the disputed words. Many classical scholars, among them Ibn Kathir and Qadi Iyad, rejected the story because of its chains of transmission, while Ibn Hajar judged that its many routes pointed to a real basis. It should be presented as debated, not as settled.

The Quran's own comment is Surah 22:52: 'We did not send before you any messenger or prophet but that, when he recited, Satan cast into his recitation; then God abolishes what Satan casts, and makes his verses firm.' However it is read, the verse admits that a prophet's recitation can contain words that are not from God.

If the report is true, the theological problem has two sides. First: if Muhammad could not distinguish divine revelation from Satanic interference, even temporarily, then the entire Quran is placed under suspicion. Muhammad's own uncertainty about the source of his revelations (upon receiving the first revelation, he feared he was possessed by a jinn) demonstrates that Quranic authentication rests on Muhammad's own fallible discernment. Second: the incident occurred precisely when Muhammad needed political accommodation with the Meccan establishment. The 'revelation' endorsing polytheism conveniently resolved that pressure; its retraction came when the political calculus shifted. This pattern (revelations coinciding with Muhammad's personal needs, later revised) recurs throughout the Quran. Deuteronomy 18:20-22 provides the prophet test: a true prophet does not speak for Satan. If the report is true, the tradition's own record raises that question sharply.
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari (prostration at the end of Surah 53)
Shahab Ahmed, Before Orthodoxy: The Satanic Verses in Early Islam (2017)
rejoinder: That is a serious reply, which is why this faultline is marked as debated. Two points remain. A story this embarrassing is hard to explain as an invention by early Muslim historians who revered Muhammad. And even if the incident is set aside, 22:52 still says that Satan casts into the recitation of every prophet, which leaves the listener depending on the prophet's own report of which words were removed.

title: Muhammad's Prophetic Credentials
summary: Muhammad claimed to be the final and greatest prophet, yet by the criteria Islam itself acknowledges for authentic prophethood, his credentials are uniquely weak: no public miracles, verifiably false predictions, and private revelations with no independent confirmation.
challenge: The Quran is the miracle: its challenge to produce a surah like it (2:23, 17:88) still stands. Hadith collections report many further signs, such as water flowing from Muhammad's fingers, and Surah 54:1 speaks of the moon being split. The Quran foretold the Byzantine recovery after their defeat by Persia (30:2-4), and it happened. Muhammad's character and the spread of his message are signs in themselves.
response:
The Islamic claim that the Quran is Muhammad's sole miracle is a position adopted after the fact, and it directly contradicts the pattern of prophetic authentication in the Scripture that predates Islam. Moses performed public miracles before Pharaoh and all Egypt. Elijah called down fire before 450 prophets of Baal and all Israel. Jesus performed miracles before hostile witnesses. The Pharisees did not deny the miracles but attributed them to Beelzebub. These are publicly verifiable, hostile-audience-attested signs. Muhammad, by his own acknowledgement, was not given such signs. Sahih Bukhari 9.92.379 records him saying: 'Every prophet was given miracles because of which people believed, but what I have been given is Divine Inspiration which Allah has revealed to me.' This is an admission that his credentials differ fundamentally from every prior prophet he claims succession from.

On failed prophecy: Surah 30:2-4 predicts Roman victory within 'bida' years (3-9 years) after a Persian defeat. The timeline was marginal at best and required post-hoc stretching. More significantly, hadith record Muhammad predicting specific companions would enter Paradise: predictions later contradicted when those companions apostatized. Predictions requiring revision are not divine prophecy.

The i'jaz argument is circular: the Quran is miraculous because no one has matched it; no one has matched it because the Quran defines what a match looks like. This is unfalsifiable. Pre-Islamic Arabic poetry achieves comparable literary heights by the assessment of non-Muslim Arabic scholars. Divine origin cannot be verified by literary excellence, which is always culturally and aesthetically conditioned. The Christian verification is categorically different: not 'this text is beautiful therefore divine' but 'this man was publicly executed and publicly raised from the dead in a historically datable event before witnesses.' These are different kinds of evidence, and only one is historically testable.
sources: Nabeel Qureshi, Seeking Allah Finding Jesus (2014)
rejoinder: Literary excellence is hard to measure and was never the test given for earlier prophets. The biblical tests are faithfulness to earlier revelation and fulfilled prediction (Deuteronomy 13:1-5, 18:21-22). The Quran itself records opponents asking Muhammad for signs and being told that signs are with God (6:109, 29:50), and many commentators also read 54:1 as concerning the Last Day. The Byzantine prediction is real but general: victory 'within a few years' (bid' sinin, three to nine) after a defeat everyone knew about, and the passage has a variant reading that reverses who is defeated.

title: The Marriage to Aisha
summary: Muhammad's marriage to Aisha (consummated when she was nine years old by the testimony of Sahih Bukhari and Sahih Muslim) creates an irresolvable moral contradiction at the heart of Islam's claim that Muhammad is the perfect ethical exemplar for all times and places.
challenge: Marriage age must be judged by the standards of its time and place, where betrothal and marriage around puberty were common across many cultures, including the ancient Near East. None of Muhammad's contemporaries, including his fiercest enemies, objected. Aisha became one of the great scholars of early Islam and spoke of her marriage with affection. Some modern Muslim writers also argue from the age of her sister Asma and from other chronology that she was older than the hadith state.
response:
The historical record is not in dispute within Islam's own most authoritative sources. Sahih Bukhari (5.58.234) records Aisha saying: 'The Prophet married me when I was six years old and consummated his marriage when I was nine years old.' Sahih Muslim (8.3309, 8.3310, 8.3311) records the same with multiple chains of transmission. These are not peripheral hadith. They are in the two collections Sunni Islam regards as most sahih after the Quran itself. The attempts to revise Aisha's age upward have not been accepted by mainstream Islamic scholarship precisely because they work against the most authoritative tradition.

The relativist defence is categorically unavailable to Islam. Islam does not present Muhammad as a man of his time. Islam presents Muhammad as al-uswa al-hasana, the beautiful pattern (Quran 33:21), whose conduct is binding sunnah for every Muslim in every culture and century. Quran 59:7 commands: 'Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it.' If Muhammad's example is context-dependent (if portions can be set aside as historically conditioned), then the entire sunnah loses its obligatory character and Sharia law loses its divine grounding. The relativist defence destroys Islam's own legal architecture to escape a moral objection.

The moral intuition that this represents a genuine problem is not Western cultural imperialism. It is the universal human recognition, cross-cultural and pre-modern, that a nine-year-old child cannot meaningfully consent to a sexual relationship with a 54-year-old man. Jesus' treatment of children (Mark 10:14-16) and his severe warning against those who harm 'these little ones' (Matthew 18:6) provides a direct and opposite standard. The question is whether Muhammad's authenticated conduct reflects the character of a man guided by the all-holy God.
rejoinder: The age is not an anti-Muslim invention: it is Aisha's own report in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, the collections Sunni Islam treats as most reliable, and the modern re-datings work by setting those sources aside. Christians need not judge seventh-century Arabia by modern law. The issue is the Quran's claim that Muhammad is an 'excellent example' (33:21) for all people and times: a timeless example cannot be defended by appeal to the customs of one time.

title: Can God's Love Be Eternal Without Another?
summary: In the Ash'ari school, the most influential in Sunni theology, God's will determines what is good, and his love for creatures is an expression of that will. Christians press a deeper question that applies to any strictly unitarian God: if love needs a beloved, whom did God love before creation? The Trinity answers it. Tawhid, as Islam defines it, struggles to.
challenge: God is al-Wadud, the Loving (85:14), and al-Rahman, the Merciful, the name that opens almost every surah. In Sunni theology God's attributes are eternal, so his love is not something he acquired at creation. God is also al-Ghani, the Self-Sufficient: he does not need a beloved in order to be perfect, and the Christian argument quietly makes God dependent on relationship.
response:
This is not a claim that Muslims have no loving God. The Quran calls God al-Wadud, the Loving (85:14), and Muslims know him as merciful. The question is what love means when it is said of God, and whether it belongs to who God eternally is.

In the Ash'ari school, the most influential in Sunni theology, what is good is good because God wills it, and God's love for creatures expresses his will towards them. Al-Ghazali argued that God would not be unjust even if he punished those who had not sinned, because justice is defined by what God does. The Maturidi school, the other main Sunni tradition, gives more weight to God's wisdom (hikma), so the point should not be pressed as true of all Islam. Across Sunni theology, though, the Quran's language of love is mostly directed at those who do good (2:195, 3:31), and 'God does not love the disbelievers' (3:32).

The Christian answer: God's own nature IS the standard of goodness. He cannot lie because he is Truth. He cannot be cruel because he is Love. His commands express what he is, not arbitrary sovereign decisions. This is not a minor nuance. It is the difference between a God whose character is the anchor of all moral reality and a God whose will is the only moral reality, which is indistinguishable from divine power.

The deeper problem concerns love itself. 1 John 4:8 does not say God loves. It says 'God IS love.' Love is not an attribute God has; it is what God is in his very being. But love requires an object. If God is eternally love (before creation, before any creature), then there must be an eternal object of love within the Godhead. This is the Trinity: the Father loving the Son in the eternal fellowship of the Spirit. Islamic tawhid (absolute divine unity without internal differentiation) means that before creation, Allah had no one to love. On this view love is something God shows to creatures, not who he eternally is. The Christian claim is different: 'God is love' (1 John 4:8), because the Father loved the Son 'before the foundation of the world' (John 17:24).
sources: Alvin Plantinga, Does God Have a Nature? (1980)
Peter Kreeft, Between Allah and Jesus (2010)
rejoinder: The Self-Sufficiency point is the strongest reply, and Christians agree that God needs nothing. That is exactly the Trinitarian claim: God's love is not a need met by creation, because the Father, the Son and the Spirit have loved one another eternally (John 17:24). The question for tawhid is what an eternal attribute of love is love for before anything else existed, if it is not simply God's will to benefit creatures who did not yet exist.

title: The Quran's Borrowed Sources
summary: The Quran contains detailed parallels with apocryphal Christian and Jewish texts circulating in 7th-century Arabia, including texts that contain demonstrable legendary material. If the Quran is God's eternal word, why does it reproduce the specific errors of human apocryphal literature?
challenge: The Quran openly retells earlier stories: it calls itself a confirmation of the scripture before it (5:48), and it addressed people who already knew these accounts. Shared stories show that the same events were known in more than one community, and the Quran often corrects them rather than copying them. Muhammad, described as unlettered (7:157), had no library of apocrypha. Similarity is not the same as dependence.
response:
The borrowing argument does not point to thematic parallels. It identifies specific, traceable narrative details from apocryphal texts that reappear in the Quran, including details that are demonstrably legendary rather than historical.

Surah 19:29-33 describes the infant Jesus speaking from the cradle, and Surah 3:49 (with 5:110) describes the boy Jesus making birds from clay that come to life. The cradle speech parallels the Syriac Infancy Gospel, preserved in Arabic as the Arabic Infancy Gospel; the clay birds come from the Infancy Gospel of Thomas (2nd century). The church had set both aside as legend, not apostolic testimony. If the Quran is God's eternal word correcting Christian error, why does it repeat material the church itself had already set aside?

Surah 18:9-26 contains the story of the People of the Cave: seven sleepers who awoke after centuries. This is a direct parallel to the Legend of the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus, a Christian legend that circulated widely in Syria and Arabia in the 6th century. The Syriac text (Jacob of Sarug, c. 474-521 AD) predates the Quran by over a century.

Surah 5:32, often quoted as a peace verse, says that killing one soul is like killing all mankind, and it introduces this as something 'We decreed for the Children of Israel.' A Muslim will rightly say the Quran is citing earlier revelation. But the saying is not in the Torah. It is rabbinic commentary on Cain's murder of Abel, recorded in the Mishnah (Sanhedrin 4:5, compiled around 200 AD), and the Quran places it directly after its own account of Cain and Abel (5:27-31). The Quran presents a rabbinic interpretation as a divine decree.

The 'unlettered' (ummi) defence does not resolve the problem; it sharpens it. Stories that circulated orally in Syriac Christian and Jewish communities could reach Arabia without any books. Muslim sources themselves record Muhammad's contacts with Christians, among them Waraqah ibn Nawfal, Khadijah's cousin, who according to Sahih al-Bukhari 3 used to write out the Gospel. Oral tradition, drawing on apocryphal and rabbinic material, is the simplest explanation for these specific parallels.
sources: Surah 19:29-33 and the Syriac (Arabic) Infancy Gospel
Surah 3:49 and the Infancy Gospel of Thomas 2
Gabriel Said Reynolds, The Qur'an and Its Biblical Subtext (2010)
rejoinder: Agreed: similarity alone proves nothing, and the Quran does retell. The problem is which stories it presents as fact. When the material is recognisable legend (the clay birds of a second-century infancy gospel, a rabbinic comment presented as a divine decree), the question is not whether Muhammad owned books but why an eternal, uncreated word would endorse the legends of a later age.

title: Islam's Self-Defeating Account of Jesus
summary: Islam affirms enough about Jesus (sinless, born of a virgin, miracle-worker, Messiah, who will return) to make its denial of his crucifixion and resurrection not just historically indefensible but internally self-contradicting. The Islamic Jesus demands Christian conclusions.
challenge: The Quran honours Jesus more than any faith outside Christianity: Messiah, a Word from God, a Spirit from Him, born of a virgin, sinless, a worker of miracles, and coming again. Raising him to Himself (4:158) rather than letting his enemies kill him is God's vindication of his prophet. Being sinless, miraculous or virgin-born does not make anyone divine: Adam had neither father nor mother (3:59).
response:
Islam's affirmations about Jesus are precisely what makes its denials theologically catastrophic, not merely wrong but self-refuting. Islam has handed Christianity its most powerful evidence and then tried to suppress the conclusion the evidence demands.

The Quran uses the title Messiah (al-Masih) for Jesus 11 times, yet provides no explanation of what Messiah means. In the Hebrew prophetic tradition the term comes from, Messiah means the anointed deliverer who redeems through suffering, death, and vindication: Isaiah 53 is the defining text. Islam uses the title while amputating the meaning. This is not theological refinement. It is incoherence.

The Quran affirms Jesus was sinless: described as a 'pure boy' (Surah 19:19). This is unparalleled in the Quran. Muhammad himself is repeatedly instructed to seek forgiveness (Surah 40:55, 47:19; Sahih Bukhari records him seeking forgiveness 70 times daily). Jesus alone has no sin. But a sinless person's death demands theological explanation. In Christian theology, death entered through sin (Romans 5:12), so the sinless Christ's death is not his own penalty but ours, borne voluntarily. Islam affirms his sinlessness but provides no account of what his death means or why it happens.

The Quran affirms Jesus raised the dead (Surah 3:49), a miracle Muhammad never performed. Islam insists Muhammad is greater. By what criterion is a prophet who performed no miracles, who could not guarantee his own salvation, greater than the sinless, miracle-working, virgin-born Messiah? The internal hierarchy of Islam's own claims does not support the ranking it assigns.

Finally: every major hadith collection records that Jesus will return before the Day of Judgment to defeat evil and establish justice. But this return has no narrative logic in Islam. In Christianity, Jesus ascended after resurrection to the Father's right hand. He will return because he left in a theologically meaningful way. In Islam, Jesus was taken up without dying and will return to die a natural death. Islam has kept the eschatological role (cosmic judge and defeater of evil) while abolishing the credentials that justify it.
rejoinder: Each title is real, and that is the problem. 'Messiah' and 'Word' had settled meanings when the Quran adopted them, and the Quran gives them no new content of its own. And the vindication reading of 4:157 asks us to accept that God made the crucifixion appear to happen, so that the apostles, the church and hostile historians all reported a real death that was an illusion. That would make God the author of the very misunderstanding Islam came to correct.

title: How Early Is the Islamic Account?
summary: Islam's detailed account of its origins (Muhammad's life, the Meccan setting, the collecting of the Quran) comes mainly from sources written 120 to 250 years later. The earliest physical evidence confirms that Islam and Muhammad's central place in it are early, but it also shows a text and a community still taking shape, which sits uneasily with claims of perfect, unbroken preservation.
challenge: The early evidence supports the tradition. The Dome of the Rock (691) names Muhammad as the messenger of God several times. Coins struck around 685-686 carry the declaration that Muhammad is God's messenger. The Birmingham Quran folios have been radiocarbon dated to roughly 568-645, close to Muhammad's lifetime. Early mosque orientations that miss Mecca reflect the limits of seventh-century astronomy, not a different holy city. And Islamic reports were transmitted with chains of narrators (isnad) precisely so that they could be checked.
response:
The text of the Quran: Muslim tradition itself records that the caliph Uthman (ruled 644-656) produced a standard copy and ordered other copies burned (Sahih al-Bukhari 4987). The Sana'a palimpsest, an early Quran manuscript whose erased lower text differs from the standard text in wording and verse order, shows that other forms circulated. The Quran's textual history is early and real, but it is a history of standardisation, not of a single text preserved without variation from the beginning.

The life of Muhammad: the earliest full biography, by Ibn Ishaq (died c. 767), was written about 120 years after Muhammad's death and survives only through later editors such as Ibn Hisham (died 833) and al-Tabari. The canonical hadith collections of al-Bukhari (died 870) and Muslim (died 875) were compiled more than two centuries after the events. Muslim scholars developed careful methods for testing chains of narrators, but the distance remains.

Compare the New Testament: Paul's letters were written within about 20 to 30 years of the crucifixion, the Gospels within the first century, and the creed in 1 Corinthians 15:3-7 within a few years of the events. Christians can make that comparison with confidence, without overstating what archaeology shows about early Islam.
sources: Behnam Sadeghi & Mohsen Goudarzi, 'San'a' 1 and the Origins of the Qur'an', Der Islam 87 (2012)
Keith Small, Textual Criticism and Qur'an Manuscripts (2011)
Fred Donner, Muhammad and the Believers (2010)
University of Birmingham, radiocarbon dating of the Birmingham Quran folios (2015)
rejoinder: All of that is fair, and Christians should concede it: Islam was early, and Muhammad was central to it from the first decades. Theories that relocate Islam's origins (for example to Petra) have not persuaded historians, and Christians weaken their case by repeating them. The real question is narrower: how early and how firm are the sources for the detailed claims Islam makes about its scripture and its prophet?
